content_text: The Cannes Film Festival, a film festival created in 1946 based on an idea by Jean Zay and called the Festival international du film until 2002, is one of the most prestigious and famous film festivals in the world. It takes place every year in May in the French city of Cannes. The "film market" (marché du film) runs alongside the festival.

In the late 1930s, shocked by the interference of the German and Italian fascist governments in the selection of films for the Venice Film Festival, Jean Zay, the Minister of Public Education and Fine Arts, proposed creating an international film festival in Cannes. In June 1939, Louis Lumière agreed to be president of the festival's first edition, which was to take place from September 1 to 30.

The declaration of war on Germany by France and the United Kingdom on September 3 put a premature end to that plan, although the award was given to Union Pacific, by Cecil B. DeMille. The festival's first edition actually took place in 1946. The festival was not held in 1948 and 1950 due to financial problems. In 1955, the organizing committee introduced the Palme d'Or as the event's main award; before then, it was known as the Grand Prix du Festival international du Film.

The 1968 festival was halted on May 19. The day before, Louis Malle, who had resigned from the jury, François Truffaut, Claude Berri, Jean-Gabriel Albicocco, Claude Lelouch, Roman Polanski and Jean-Luc Godard had stormed into the Palais' main theater and demanded that the screenings be stopped in solidarity with the striking workers and students.

The Palme d'Or: the most prestigious award of the Cannes Film Festival, presented since 1955 to the Festival's winning film. The annual choice is made by a jury of international film professionals from among films submitted from many parts of the world, and takes place in May in the city of Cannes, on the French Riviera. Some of the most notable directors in film history have seen their films honored on different occasions. One of the most important and prestigious film awards in the world (its current design was created by designer Caroline Scheufele-Gruosi and has been used since 1997), the Palme d'Or was first awarded to the American film Marty, by Delbert Mann, and since then it was only not presented between 1964 and 1974, when it was replaced by the Grand Prix, the award that, until 1954, was given at Cannes as the main prize, and that is still awarded today, under the name Grand Prix du Juri, to films honored with a symbolic second place. Thus, only the films awarded between 1955 and 1963 and from 1975 to the present day are officially considered Palme d'Or winners. In May 1968, when a wave of student protests broke out in Paris and spread throughout France, the Festival was canceled and no awards were given.

The Short Film Palme d'Or (Palme d'or du court métrage) : the most prestigious short film award of the Cannes Film Festival, presented since 1953 by the Cinéfondation to the Festival's best short film. Sometimes a "special mention" or the Jury Prize is given to other notable short films of that particular year.
The Grand Prix : an award for which the jury chooses the best film. It is the festival's second most respected award, surpassed only by the Palme d'Or.
Jury Prize (Prix du jury) : an annual honor presented at the Cannes Film Festival to films awarded by the jury since 1946.

Best Actress (Prix d'interprétation féminine) : also known as the Palme d'Or for Best Actress, it is one of the awards presented by the jury of the official section of the Cannes Film Festival. The festival was conceived in 1939 on the initiative of Jean Zay, the French Minister of Public Education and Fine Arts. The first edition took place in 1946 and, since then, it has brought together big names of the seventh art in the French resort town of Cannes, on the Côte d'Azur, the French Riviera. It is the most prestigious film event in the world. The Prix d'interprétation féminine is dedicated to the best female performance among the films competing for the Palme d'Or, and has been awarded since the first edition, when Frenchwoman Michèle Morgan received the honor, at age 26, for her role in La Symphonie Pastorale (Pastoral Symphony, 1946). This award has seen a large number of ties, many for the same film. In 1981, Frenchwoman Isabelle Adjani pulled off the feat of tying with herself, thus winning two awards in a single edition. English actress Jodhi May was the youngest actress to receive the honor, at age 12, for her performance in A World Apart (1988). American actresses are the most awarded (21 wins), followed by the host country's French actresses (17). More than 84 actresses from various countries have been honored.

Best Actor (Prix d'interprétation masculine) : a trophy awarded at the Cannes Film Festival to the best actor. The winner is chosen by a jury of the Festival's official film section. The award was first presented in 1946.

Best Director (Prix de la mise en scène) : an award presented at the Cannes Film Festival to the best film director. The winner is chosen by the jury of the festival's official film section. It was first presented in 1946.

content_text: Best Screenplay (Prix du scénario) : an award presented at the Cannes Film Festival by a jury of the official film section. It was first presented in 1949.
The Short Film Jury Prize (Prix du jury du court métrage) : an annual honor presented at the Cannes Film Festival to films awarded by the jury since 1946.
Golden Camera (Caméra d'or) : rewards the best first film from all of these sections.

The Trophée Chopard (Breakthrough Performance Award) : a Cannes Film Festival award dedicated each year to encouraging new talent in film. It was founded in 2001 by Chopard, and since then a jury has decided every year which of the new talents presented at the Festival is the most promising.

title: From 2021 to 2026
description:
In 2020, for the first time since 1968, the Cannes Film Festival did not take place. Scheduled for May 12 to 23, the 73rd edition was canceled because of the COVID-19 pandemic: there was no competition and no Palme d'Or. In June the festival announced an Official Selection under the "Cannes 2020" label, without competing for awards, and in October it held a small event on the Croisette, where only the Short Film Palme d'Or (to I Am Afraid to Forget Your Face, by Sameh Alaa) and the Cinéfondation prizes were presented. Spike Lee, who had been invited to preside over the 2020 jury, presided over the 2021 one.

The 2021 edition was postponed from May to July (July 6 to 17), the only time in the period that the festival moved out of May. From 2022 on, Cannes returned to its usual calendar and began creating awards outside the traditional categories whenever the jury wanted to highlight a film: the 75th Anniversary Prize (2022) and the Special Prize (officially "Prix Spécial", in 2024 and 2025). Ties (ex-æquo) also became common: the Grand Prix was shared in 2021 and 2022, the Jury Prize in 2021, 2022 and 2025, and the Best Director award in 2026.
